title: Leading Wildcard LIKE Can't Seek
description: LIKE '%term%' can't seek because of the leading wildcard; an anchored 'term%' pattern becomes a range seek. Why it matters: "search contains" is one of the most requested features in any app, and a leading wildcard is the classic, easy-to-miss reason it doesn't scale.
narrative:
## Scenario
To find usernames beginning with `admin`, the query uses `WHERE Username LIKE '%admin%'`. Even though `Username` is indexed, the plan is a full **Index Scan** of all 200,000 rows.

## Why it's slow
An index is sorted left-to-right, so a `LIKE` pattern is only seekable **up to its first wildcard**. `'%admin%'` starts with `%` — there is no left anchor, so SQL Server cannot pick a starting point in the index and must examine **every** row. A leading wildcard defeats the index exactly the way wrapping the column in a function does.

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** on a column that has a perfectly good index.
- A `LIKE` pattern that begins with `%` (or `_`).

## The concept
If you only need a **prefix** match, drop the leading `%`: `LIKE 'admin%'`. A fixed prefix gives the optimizer a left anchor, which it turns into a **range seek** (`>= 'admin'` and `< 'admio'`) — reads collapse from ~600 to a handful. (If you genuinely need a *contains* search, that's what full-text indexing is for; a plain b-tree index can't seek an interior substring.)
startingQuery: SELECT UserId, Username FROM Users WHERE Username LIKE '%admin%';
hints: An index can only be seeked up to the first wildcard in the pattern.
A pattern starting with % has no left anchor, so SQL Server must scan every row.
If you only need a prefix match, use LIKE 'admin%' so the index can range-seek.
